B. Use a Reach or Throw rescue from the dock first - lie flat on the dock and extend a rescue pole, paddle, towel, or ring buoy so the rescuer stays out of the water.

D. Have two non-swimmer buddies form a human chain in 8-foot water without wearing PFDs.

pamphlet_excerpts: Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check: Conscious victims probably can remove themselves from the water once they have sure footing on the bottom or a firm hold on a ladder (p. 57).
Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check Principle 2: Choose a safe landing site before entering the water (p. 57).
Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check Principle 3: In exceptional cases, such as in a steep-sided quarry, you may both need help from others onshore (p. 57).
Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check Principle 4: When landing a conscious victim, lower your legs to check the water depth if you can do so without causing the victim to lose support (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): Natural bodies of water can be shallow for long distances from shore (p. 57).
Step 2 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): It may be easier to walk through shallow water than it is to swim (p. 57).
Step 3 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): If the victim is exhausted, cold, or has trouble with footing, help him or her ashore using a shallow-water assist (p. 57).
Step 4 (Prerequisite Swimming Endurance Check): While standing at the person's side, help him or her to stand and to place one arm around your neck and across your shoulder (p. 57).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (It Is Appropriate to Remove): Natural bodies of water can be shallow for long distances from shore (p. 54).

Step 3 (It Is Appropriate to Remove): If the victim is exhausted, cold, or has trouble with footing, help him or her ashore using a shallow-water assist (p. 54).
Step 4 (It Is Appropriate to Remove): While standing at the person's side, help him or her to stand and to place one arm around your neck and across your shoulder (p. 54).

pamphlet_excerpts: Importance of Avoiding Contact: If an active victim will not follow you to shore, back off and wait (p. 59).
Importance of Avoiding Contact Principle 2: The person may become more cooperative as he orshe tires (p. 59).

Importance of Avoiding Contact Principle 3: As long as the victim can keep his or her head above water, the water is warm, and no currents are carrying you toward danger, you are not forced to act (p. 59).
Importance of Avoiding Contact Principle 4: Stay close enough to place the victim in a tow if it becomes necessary (p. 59).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Importance of Avoiding Contact): In rare cases you may need to provide assistance to someone by supporting them without a flotation device (p. 59).
Step 2 (Importance of Avoiding Contact): One such circumstance is if you and others are caught in a rip current and some of the party become increasingly tired trying to swim (p. 59).
Step 3 (Importance of Avoiding Contact): For short distances, you can aid a cooperative tired person swimming on his or her stomach by swimming alongside and grasping the upper arm (p. 59).
Step 4 (Importance of Avoiding Contact): If the person is trying a restful backstroke, a single armpittow is appropriate (p. 59).

Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry Principle 2: Whenever possible, use a flotation aid to help support both you and a passive victim (p. 30).
Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry Principle 3: If a suitable aid is not available, try either the wrist tow or the armpit tows (p. 30).
Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry Principle 4: However, both of those maybe ineffective in some cases (p. 30).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry): Since a victim recovered from the bottom is no longer floating, you will need to provide additional support while swimming (p. 30).
Step 2 (Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry): The relaxed neck muscles of an unconscious victim may make it difficult to keep his or her faceout of the water, particularly in rough water (p. 30).
Step 3 (Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry): The cross-chest carry, or tow, gives a victim additional support and can be used if other techniques prove difficult (p. 30).
Step 4 (Transitions to Cross-Chest Carry): Changing from armpittow to cross-chest tow Changing from wrist towto cross-chest tow You can change to a cross-chest tow from either the armpit tow (p. 30).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): In rare cases you may need to provide assistance to someone by supporting them without a flotation device (p. 60).
Step 2 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): One such circumstance is if you and others are caught in a rip current and some of the party become increasingly tired trying to swim (p. 60).
Step 3 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): For short distances, you can aid a cooperative tired person swimming on his or her stomach by swimming alongside and grasping the upper arm (p. 60).
Step 4 (Contact Assists for Active Victims): If the person is trying a restful backstroke, a single armpittow is appropriate (p. 60).

pamphlet_excerpts: Management of a spinal injury: Diving into shallow or unclear water is unsafe and foolish (p. 85).
Management of a spinal injury Principle 2: The diver risks spinal injury, permanent paralysis, or death (p. 85).
Management of a spinal injury Principle 3: In pools, most diving injuries happen in shallow water but also can occurif the diver hits another swimmer or a diving board (p. 85).
Management of a spinal injury Principle 4: In lakes and rivers, diving injuries are caused by misjudging the depth of the water or hitting rocks or trees unseen from the surface (p. 85).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Management of a spinal injury): At beaches, lunging into waves or falling off a board can cause spinal injury when a wave slams the victim into the bottom (p. 85).
Step 2 (Management of a spinal injury): If you notice anyone dive into the water and float immobile to the surface, call for help immediately (p. 85).
Step 3 (Management of a spinal injury): Head, neck, and spinal injuries are extremely serious and are best handled by trained personnel with special equipment (p. 85).
Step 4 (Management of a spinal injury): If trained and equipped personnel are not immediately available, your job is to maintain the person in a faceup stable position until help (p. 85).
